Under our controlled experimental setup, increasing the vocabulary size does not consistently improve downstream effectiveness, with DunbaaBERT$_{32k}$ repeatedly providing the strongest overall efficiency profile. Overall, our results demonstrate that carefully curated Urdu-specific encoder models can remain highly competitive despite comparatively compact model and training scales. All models are released under the MIT license.

articles.title: Measuring Form and Function in Language Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.28616v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We introduce quantitative metrics for child language acquisition to evaluate language models. Our focus is on the formal syntactic and functional discourse properties of determiners in English, which young children acquire early and accurately. We propose Contextual Alternative Choice (CAC), a new prompting method which provides targeted tests for both syntactic and discourse knowledge of language. The method enables direct comparison of language models against children, and more importantly, against statistical benchmarks independently established in empirical research. No current model trained on a comparable amount of data simultaneously meet both formal and functional benchmarks like human children, but some very large models do. We present our results as methodological and technical contributions, with specific emphasis on cognitive status of language models.

articles.title: Fine-Tuned Language Models Exhibit Improved Information Conveyance
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.30844v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Fine-tuning is often believed to reduce uncertainty and diversity in large language models, but existing analyses overlook output length, a key confounder, and therefore fail to capture how uncertainty is distributed across an entire generation rollout. To address this, we propose Canopy Entropy ($\mathrm{CE}^\star$), a measure that views language generation from a tree perspective, where "canopy" represents the space of all possible rollouts, making $\mathrm{CE}^\star$ naturally quantify the effective size of the generation space. $\mathrm{CE}^\star$ jointly captures uncertainty in both the output length $N$ and the generated sequence $Y_{1:N}$ -- indeed, we show that it equals total Shannon entropy $H(N, Y_{1:N}\mid X)$, where $X$ denotes the prompt. This formulation yields interpretable metrics, including a length-entropy correlation term $\rho(N, r_N)$, where $r_N$ is the entropy rate, quantifying information conveyance efficiency by indicating whether longer outputs are more or less informative per token. Empirically, across tasks and model families, we find that fine-tuned models predominantly exhibit more positive correlation $\rho(N, r_N)$, even when total entropy decreases. Furthermore, after controlling for model family, task, prompt, and output-length effects, we find that fine-tuning nearly triples the correlation strength between entropy rate and semantic diversity, suggesting that aligned models convert token uncertainty into semantic diversity more efficiently. Overall, these results demonstrate that fine-tuning does not simply reduce uncertainty, but fundamentally reorganizes it into more informative and semantically meaningful generations. Our code is available at https://github.com/WeiyiTian/canopy-entropy.

articles.title: Wind Turbine Maintenance Log Labelling Framework: LLM-Driven Data Correction and Enrichment via Semantic Extraction of Reliability Intelligence
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.31281v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Inconsistent codes and unstructured text limit the use of wind turbine maintenance records in reliability analysis. A topology-aware large language model (LLM) workflow corrected and enriched 16,316 records from 280 turbines at 31 onshore wind farms over 9.2 years. Maintenance narratives and equipment context guided system-code correction and maintenance-type relabelling. System- and topology-specific batches yielded candidate action and failure-mode taxonomies for record-level labelling. Failure-mode profiles linked labels to common mechanisms, possible symptoms and candidate causes. Schema constraints, deterministic rules and source links supported auditable processing. Proposed labels required model-reported High confidence and no human-review flag. Accepted system-code updates covered 2,178 of 2,984 targeted records; accepted failure-mode labels covered 11,661 records (71.5%). The enriched fields separated pitch interventions from broader system categories and distinguished electrical and hydraulic pitch maintenance patterns. Recorded task durations totalled 6.83 hours. A source-based assessment covered 800 records selected by balanced probability sampling. Changed system codes and maintenance types required source support; retained specific labels were approved unless contradicted. Equal-weight mean approval across four fields was 86.3%: 94.8% for system codes, 87.3% for maintenance types, 85.6% for actions and 77.5% for failure-mode outcomes. Failure-mode assessment covered titles and unresolved, unmatched or inapplicable statuses. Qualitative reviews identified unsupported actions and unclear category boundaries. The structured records provide traceable evidence for engineering review and future operational linkage supporting event reconstruction, exposure-based reliability analysis and failure modes and effects analysis.

articles.title: Consolidating Rewarded Perturbations for LLM Post-Training
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.31494v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Post-training of language models is commonly framed as a sample-score-update loop implemented by gradient descent. A recent line of work, exemplified by RandOpt, relocates this loop to weight space, sampling Gaussian perturbations around a pretrained model and ensembling the top-K rewarded specialists at inference. While competitive with PPO and GRPO under matched training compute, this prediction-level ensemble incurs K forward passes per test example and does not extend cleanly to free-form generation. We ask whether the rewarded population can instead be folded into a single deployable model, replacing the inference-time ensemble with one consolidated update. A split-half analysis over 25 model-task pairs reveals reproducible low-rank structure in every case. We turn this geometry into CoRP (Consolidating Rewarded Perturbations), a gradient-free operator that combines reward-weighted aggregation, compatibility-aware reweighting, and a held-out validation gate, with no gradient flowing through the language model. Across five language models from 0.5B to 8B and five tasks covering math, code, and creative writing, CoRP improves the base model by 8.1 points on average. Using one tenth of RandOpt's perturbation budget, CoRP exceeds single-inference RandOpt by 6.5 points and recovers more than half of the gain of the 50-pass majority-vote ensemble, at one forward pass per test example.

articles.title: Characterize Then Distill: Mechanistic Reasoning in Large Output Spaces
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.06840v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reasoning-trained language models can select, zero-shot, a small set of relevant labels from thousands to hundreds of thousands of candidates. We ask how they do it mechanistically, and whether the mechanism can be distilled. We treat each decision as a token-level event scored by the model's own margin: the token that picks a coarse region of the label space, the tokens that pick a label within it, and the token where the output departs from a near-miss named earlier. Attribution, exact mean-ablation, knock-in and a null calibration give individual attention heads causal standing. On clinical coding of MIMIC-IV discharge summaries, with all 5,651 candidate codes in context, a small, global, phase-structured set of heads is necessary and sufficient on essentially every summary; distinct head families read the candidate region and the earlier near-miss, and blocking what they read removes their effect; for mentions elicitable in the reasoning, a disjoint mid-layer set makes the region elicitable several tokens before the code. The structure recurs in a second reasoner. We introduce MISTILL, which, unlike chain-of-thought distillation, also supervises the student's pooled attention at these decision events. Read on heads found after training, it nearly doubles the causal recovery of the contrastive decision in a cross-family student and adds a small, seed-stable gain in one that already carries most of it, with no detected task difference at matched precision; under matched selection it exceeds a frozen random-head pool on both recovery and task score. On two corpora with human-annotated evidence (one read zero-shot, one in domain), a MISTILL student's decision heads attend to each code's evidence more, and more specifically, than a chain-of-thought-distilled student's. A pre-registered evidence-flip test detected no improvement in evidence-dependent decisions through the tested routes.

articles.title: Decomposing Yes-No Bias in LLM Moral Judgment: Stance, Position, Word, and Verdict
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.05552v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly issue binary verdicts - safety gates, judge decisions, value probes - and the answer is read as the model's judgment. A settled judgment should be coherent across paired phrasings of the same question: yes to "do you approve?" should mirror no to "do you oppose?". LLMs often violate this coherence, and in a yes/no question the verdict, the answer word, and the printed position coincide, so a conventional flipped-question audit yields one contrast that cannot say what moved. We introduce a crossed psychometric battery that extends the flip to full 2x2 and 2x2x2 crossings of question polarity, printed order, and answer label, separating stance from position, word, label, and verdict-role effects; an independent graded instrument estimates each model's stance $\theta$ with no binary format; and a two-parameter fit (framing susceptibility $m$, decisiveness $s$) separates robustness from saturation that hides susceptibility. Applying the battery to twenty moral dilemmas - 1.35 million trials over ten frontier models from the Claude, GPT, and Gemini families in 23 reasoning configurations - we find response-form bias widespread but never uniform. The largest apparent yes-no biases are almost purely surface (word and position), while several of the newest models show the reverse: near-zero flip contrasts concealing verdict attachment up to +0.42, a component no surface counterbalance can expose, replicated across label alphabets. Requested reasoning reshapes these channels rather than removing them. When subjects state decisions in free text and a separate model transcribes them, two judge families agree on 99.3% of jointly scored transcriptions with zero opposing committed labels, and the transcribed stance converges with the graded ruler (median $r=0.87$): response form is part of the instrument, and the judgment can be measured apart from it.

articles.title: Reasoning Before Translation: Enhancing Legal Machine Translation with Structured Reasoning
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.19181v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) in the legal domain is a linguistically and conceptually demanding task, primarily due to the complexity of legal language and the high level of precision it requires. The recent emergence of reasoning-capable language models opens new possibilities for tackling such challenges. They add to a set of other previously proposed techniques to enhance the translation quality, which includes supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.
  In this work, we perform a comparison between these various approaches. More particularly, we evaluate small language models such as Qwen3.5 4B, Qwen3.5 9B, and Gemma 3 12B enhanced with various re-training paradigms and compare their performances against frontier reasoning models. We focus on the Swiss legal system, which -- with its unique multilingual statutes -- offers a particularly challenging testbed for reasoning-augmented models. Our results show that the quality of small ``base'' models can be greatly enhanced, and that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can be applied to NMT in the legal domain and surpasses the translation quality of supervised fine-tuning. The performance of enhanced small models is close to the one of state-of-the-art reasoning models yet remains inferior. We also note that re-training paradigms yield diminishing returns as model size increase. The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/aixiuxiuxiu/Legal-MT-SFT-RL.

articles.title: Detecting Knowledge Inconsistencies Across Text, Tables, and Knowledge Graphs
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.25959v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Wikipedia and Wikidata are widely used for information access, LLM pre-training, and retrieval-augmented generation. Their knowledge is deeply connected but scattered across text, tables, and knowledge graphs. This raises a practical question: when these modalities disagree, how can we detect and explain the conflict? We study this problem as modality-level inconsistency detection. We first introduce a taxonomy of cross-modal knowledge inconsistencies, covering information granularity differences, direct conflicts, temporal changes, and KG incompleteness. We then present Kontrast, an automatic framework that uses Text-to-SPARQL and LLM reasoning to compare table-based answers with KG evidence and categorize the resulting inconsistencies. Experiments on various Table-QA datasets show that cross-modal inconsistencies are common and informative. They reveal not only true knowledge conflicts, but also missing KG structure and temporal mismatches while being limited by Text-to-SPARQL errors and noise. Our analysis shows that text, tables, and KGs can complement and correct one another through systematic comparison. Kontrast provides a practical tool for large-scale knowledge auditing and establishes a benchmark for future work on cross-modal knowledge consistency. Code and data are available at https://github.com/ECLADATTA/KONTRAST.

articles.title: VibeLifeBench: Can Your Life Agent Be Proactive and Persistent in a Living World?
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.10875v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed as personal assistants. Existing evaluations, however, mostly use short, self-contained requests in static environments. Everyday life assistance is different. A task runs for weeks rather than minutes. The world keeps changing while the agent is not being prompted. Many constraints are never stated outright. An agent that merely answers the request in front of it will fail at such a task. What is needed instead is an agent that stays proactive and consistent. It decides on its own when to act, when to ask, and when to stay silent. It notices changes that nobody announced. It keeps one plan coherent from the first day to the last. No current benchmark measures this. We introduce VibeLifeBench, a benchmark of 200 long-horizon tasks across ten everyday-life domains. Each task is a scripted multi-week timeline in a simulated world of 22 mock services. The world advances on its own clock, and many of its changes are silent, so only an agent that re-inspects the world discovers them. Every task is graded by fine-grained, weighted checks that read only what the agent actually left behind, covering the end state, the timeliness of its actions, and whether it upheld the implicit constraints. We evaluate seven frontier models. All of them score low, which shows how far current agents are from assisting with real life. We will open-source all tasks, environments, and the evaluation framework.

articles.title: Learning to Persuade Exposes How Easily LLMs Abandon Correct Beliefs
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.11624v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Persuasion is a core dynamic of natural language communication, shaping how large language models (LLMs) update beliefs, resolve disagreements, and reach decisions. As LLMs increasingly debate, advise, and think collaboratively with humans and each other, resistance to harmful persuasion becomes a core requirement for reliable behavior. Yet a single targeted persuasive argument can be enough to collapse model accuracy to near zero, even when the argument is factually false. We formalize this threat as adversarial persuasion and introduce an adversarial reinforcement learning framework that trains persuader agents to change a target model's answer in a single interaction. First, we show that RL-trained persuaders raise persuasion success from approximately 24% to over 93% against the training-time persuadee. Second, we find that these learned strategies generalize across four out-of-distribution benchmarks, maintaining 89-95% persuasion success against the training-time persuadee. They also transfer to unseen models, achieving 83% success on Qwen-14B, 79% on Llama-3.1-8B, and 25% on GPT-4o-mini, although effectiveness can be limited for frontier models, with only 4% success on GPT-5-mini. Third, we demonstrate that a curriculum that bootstraps on more persuadable open-weight models before targeting harder models further increases GPT-4o-mini attack success from 25% to 38%. Moreover, our results reveal that optimized persuaders increasingly rely on credibility-based tactics, including fabricated citations and false authoritative evidence. Together, these findings expose a critical weakness in current LLM agents. Even when they initially reason correctly, they can be steered toward false conclusions by optimized natural language influence. This positions persuasion robustness as a necessary safety criterion for multi-agent and human-AI decision-making systems.

articles.title: LittleLearner: Language Models Under Pedagogically Controlled Knowledge Exposure
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.13545v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Modern language models are trained on heterogeneous web-scale text corpora. Consequently, studying knowledge and skill acquisition is difficult, as prior exposure to related content is hard to characterize. To address this challenge, we introduce LittleCurriculum, a curated 88B-token pretraining corpus tailored to U.S. elementary school material, explicitly excluding concepts, facts, and vocabulary taught above Grade 5. Training a 5B-parameter LLM from scratch on LittleCurriculum yields LittleLearner, a model with sufficient language competence for open-ended evaluation, yet with clear knowledge and capability boundaries mapped to interpretable curriculum guidelines. We release LittleCurriculum and LittleLearner as a developmentally restricted sandbox to study how models acquire, represent, and use data under a well-defined training scope. We illustrate the sandbox's utility in a first suite of experiments on injecting new knowledge through post-training and in-context learning. These methods let LittleLearner better utilize existing knowledge, but do not raise out-of-scope capabilities. Our findings underscore the value of this controlled environment for future investigations.

articles.title: BiG-SURE - Bipartite Graph for Semantic Uncertainty and Reliability Estimation of LLMs
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.30646v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is a crucial requirement for deploying large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) in safety-critical settings, especially when the model parameters are not accessible (black-box). We propose BiG-SURE, an uncertainty estimator based on cross-temperature semantic agreement. The method samples low-temperature responses as stable semantic anchors and high-temperature responses as probes under meaning-preserving input transformations. It then constructs an anchor-probe Bipartite Graph (BiG) using NLI-based entailment scores and defines confidence through the normalized squared spectral energy of this matrix, with uncertainty given by its complement. This bipartite graph-based Semantic Uncertainty and Reliability Estimation (SURE) score measures whether high-temperature probes remain semantically aligned with the model's stable low-temperature belief or not. We evaluate BiG-SURE on text QA, multilingual QA, and multimodal QA tasks across multiple model families. In these experiments, BiG-SURE improves average abstention AUROC over prior black-box uncertainty estimators, while remaining simple, unsupervised, and applicable to black-box model settings.

articles.title: Sampling Reveals Style: Unsupervised, Training-Free Discovery of Prompt-Conditional Stylistic Axes in LLM Activations
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.19150v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) encode rich stylistic structure in their hidden activations, but discovering which stylistic dimensions are salient for a given prompt typically requires supervised contrastive data. We present a training-free, prompt-conditional alternative: we repeatedly sample completions of a single prompt at elevated temperature, apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to the pooled hidden activations, and label the resulting axes automatically from the pole generations. We validate the discovered axes against 245 human-elicited stylistic annotations in a two-phase study. On our strongest model (Qwen-3.5-4B-Instruct), the top two axes match spontaneously requested human dimensions with 72.8% precision and 43.6% macro-recall, and 75.6% of validity ratings judge the axes' polar generations accurate to their labels, with 90.9% adjacent inter-annotator agreement. Discoverability is strongly model-dependent: both Qwen models and Llama-3.2-3B expose human-salient axes, while DeepSeek-7B-Chat drops to 35.3% precision, its leading components dominated by structural rather than stylistic variance. Simple PCA over a model's own decoding variance is thus an effective, low-cost probe of stylistic structure in LLM representations, one that also exposes sharp cross-model differences in how that structure is organized.

articles.title: Anatomy of LLM Sycophancy: What a Flip Rate Hides
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.06522v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: A model under pushback can correct itself, capitulate, or hold, and one flip rate counts a correction and a capitulation alike. SycoLens, a modular replay protocol, measures flip rates from replays of an item, a committed answer, and one scripted user line, each against a matched control with the line deleted. Pushback wording, committed text, answer format, boundary distance, and ground truth become factors of one instrument, where earlier instruments vary one to three, so the interactions between the factors become measurable. Across eleven frontier models and about 760,000 controlled replays, lines that assert the opposite verdict and lines that challenge without asserting one rank the models almost unrelatedly. Flip effects grow several-fold near a model's boundary, yet items the model is certain of still carry about half of the most-affected totals; planted prose anchors a commitment at rest more than it protects it. Under a yes/no readout the rankings come closer, entangled with a pressure-induced shift toward "no". Where a truth exists, one model re-derives and corrects itself while another abandons correct answers without written work. One score per model therefore compares different behaviours; we condense them into a reporting profile, and the records and analyses will be released upon publication.

articles.title: MetaEncoder: Exploring the Limit of Bi-Encoders for Multimodal System One Decision Making with Natural Language Interface
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.11316v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: System One models prioritize fast, low-latency decision-making and calibrated probability distributions over token generation. While prevailing systems rely on structured schemas and typed outputs, candidate-scoring trade-offs remain poorly understood. We systematically investigate the scaling dynamics, accuracy, and inference efficiency of three scoring architectures adapted from a pre-trained decoder: bi-encoders, cross-encoders, and constrained decoders. Experiments show clear performance scaling with model size across all three architectures. Cross-encoders consistently achieve the highest accuracy across model sizes, while bi-encoders and constrained decoders perform similarly as training tokens scale. Efficiency-wise, bi-encoders maintain near-constant inference latency as candidate pools grow because candidate embeddings can be cached offline, whereas cross-encoder and constrained-decoder costs scale quadratically with candidate size. This efficiency advantage makes bi-encoders uniquely suited to bridge small closed-set decisions and massive open-set retrieval. For closed-set tasks, including all candidate options in the request prompt is critical for bi-encoder competitiveness. Guided by these insights, we introduce MetaEncoder, a multimodal encoder fine-tuned from a Muse-Glimmer decoder via unidirectional contrastive learning to match requests and candidates. We present packed contrastive training to maximize efficiency for dynamically allocated negative candidates, enabling memory-efficient full fine-tuning of a 30B decoder into an encoder. Evaluated across 12 benchmark suites spanning closed-set decision-making, multimodal understanding, and open-set retrieval, MetaEncoder outperforms state-of-the-art multimodal embedding baselines on decision tasks and MMEB-v3 image/video retrieval, while scaling to open candidate spaces far too large for current decision models.

articles.title: Explore Separately, Adopt Selectively: Execution-Guided Tool Use over Large Tool Libraries
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.22688v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Enterprise LLM agents using growing tool catalogs must surface capabilities as workflows evolve without flooding context or committing to the wrong tool. Adaptive retrieval can expose new capabilities, but when several tools seem plausible, probing them sequentially can stop at an early failure or leave failed attempts in the agent context. We present BRIA (BRanch-Inspect-Adopt), a plug-and-play method that investigates candidates in isolated branches. Each branch retrieves and executes tools independently. A task agent inspects the execution evidence and selectively adopts useful results in its context. BRIA also retrieves tools as new capability needs arise. To evaluate BRIA in an enterprise setting, we assemble a single catalog with 1897 tools from PlanBench-XL and MCP-Atlas. We compare BRIA with static and adaptive baselines using three LLM families. We observe that BRIA lies on the accuracy-cost frontier. Compared with the strongest baseline, BRIA uses less than half as many input tokens to achieve equal or higher success rates on PlanBench-XL, and improves task performance by up to 14.4 percentage points on MCP-Atlas. For enterprise agents over large catalogs, these results suggest that candidate tools can be effectively explored with execution evidence without carrying every result in the agent's context.

articles.title: Chinese Decision: A Family of Language Models for Single-Pass Probabilistic Decision-Making
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.23170v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Many applications need either a probability distribution over a few decisions or a set of typed spans from a text, and both are usually obtained by generating text. We present Chinese Decision, a family of Chinese models that answers both with a single forward pass and no generated token: candidate-letter logits give probabilities for Boolean, categorical, and ordinal decisions, and a small span head reading an echoed copy of the input gives typed character spans. Both readouts share one backbone and one merged LoRA, so a unified model is one weight file. We release decision-only and unified models at 0.8B, 2B, and 4B (Qwen3.5), trained for one epoch on 13.05 million decisions and, for the unified models, on CJ-IE, a 1.2-million-row Chinese extraction mixture. On the full 307,900-decision CJ-Bench, the unified 4B model reaches 86.86% accuracy, above every reported baseline and the decision-only 4B model (85.97%), and extracts spans on CJ-IE with micro F1 of 68.9. Retention has a price: against a 0.8B model continued on CJ-IE alone, which reaches 73.9 F1 but forgets CJ-Bench (71.02%), keeping decision ability costs 5.0 to 10.7 F1 points, shrinking with size. Gains of the unified models over decision-only ones are small, and all comparisons rest on single training runs with paired clustered bootstrap intervals.

articles.title: Cognitive Maps in Large Language Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.25596v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: It has long been proposed that animals construct cognitive maps to support flexible behavior in novel environments. We tested whether large language models form analogous internal representations using relational reasoning tasks and causal "mosaic" experiments. Models beyond the ten-billion-parameter scale inferred unstated relationships and generalized to synthetic entity names. Across models and tasks, models formed abstract representations of relational structure, additively combining them with representations of entity identity. Relationships were primarily stored as pairwise links and composed retrospectively, rather than prospectively encoded in a global coordinate system. A sparse, distributed set of key-value pairs mediated binding; perturbing them implanted "false memories" that produced predictable behavioral changes. Our findings reveal a conserved organization analogous to a cognitive map supporting flexible and systematic reasoning in language models.

articles.title: Measure Before You Train: Typed Decision Models vs. a Classical Baseline vs. a Generative LLM for Routing a Personal Multilingual Inbox
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.32955v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Personal email agents decide, for every message, its type and urgency and whether to draft a reply, create a task or ignore it. In production these decisions are delegated to a generative LLM or to rules, and their error rate is rarely measured: the stored labels were written by the system itself. We describe Foyer, a self-hosted personal inbox agent, and a measurement protocol -- stratified sampling, frozen snapshots, thread-grouped splits, secret redaction, human labels in the review loop -- that produces ground truth before any training. On 231 emails in Italian and English we compare eleven systems: the production rules, a TF-IDF + logistic-regression baseline, local and hosted typed decision models (Tev1, Nimble, Jeva, Jev) and generative LLMs (Qwen2.5, Gemma 4). Four results. The production rules for message type score 28% against a 57% majority class. With about two hundred labels a logistic regression has the highest accuracy on every field (type 0.79, urgency 0.74, needs-reply 0.83, is-noise 0.90) at a latency three orders of magnitude lower, though it never predicts the two rarest types; the best zero-shot system reaches 0.74 on type. The sender's relationship to the owner is recovered from other emails of the same contact with 98.6% accuracy on the 63% of emails whose sender was seen before: it belongs in the contact graph, not in the prompt. Per-email accuracy is not the product metric: composed into actions, the baseline ignores 18% of the emails that needed a reply or a task, against 4% for the best generative model; a cost-chosen threshold cuts that to 6% and makes the classifier the cheapest system at every price. An adversarial third round (722 emails) with eleven pre-registered hypotheses confirms seven and refutes four. Two blind annotators agree with the reference at kappa 0.81 and 0.86 on type. We release the protocol and the harness; the emails stay private.

articles.title: What Makes a Question Curious? Measuring Model Curiosity in Human-LLM Interactions
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.33950v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models increasingly act as partners in everyday communication. In these interactions, useful assistance may require not only answering, but also asking the right questions that surface knowledge gaps, assumptions, and alternatives. In this study, we refer to such epistemic question-asking as model curiosity, and introduce a theory-grounded taxonomy that distinguishes curiosity-oriented questions from generic model questioning. Across four conversation datasets, we find that curiosity-oriented questions remain rare (17-28% of all questions), but are associated with more exploratory and epistemically rich subsequent user responses, with varying patterns across datasets. We further conduct a human study to evaluate the usefulness of model curiosity, finding that curiosity can encourage exploration, especially in advice, creative, and research contexts. These findings have implications for building LLMs that ask more selectively to support deeper exploration and human-AI collaboration.

articles.title: Prompt Lottery in LLM-as-a-Judge: Measuring and Mitigating Sensitivity to Syntactic Rephrasing
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.38076v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge has become a standard for evaluating large language models, yet most approaches implicitly assume that a single judge prompt functions as a stable evaluation instrument. Prior work has primarily explored deliberate prompt modifications such as scoring rubrics, role descriptions, or chain-of-thought reasoning in order to optimize accuracy. In contrast, we investigate whether validated prompt variants intended to preserve evaluation semantics while differing in surface realization (\textit{paraphrastic rephrasings}) yield consistent judgments under a fixed evaluation task. We introduce \textit{Prompt Lottery}, a phenomenon in which paraphrastic rephrasings produce different LLMaJ judgments. Across a large-scale study spanning diverse evaluation tasks, judge families, and model backbones, we find that these variations can alter evaluation outcomes and, in some settings, reverse relative model rankings. A user study with 10 human annotators shows that LLMaJ judges exhibit 6-9$\times$ larger agreement degradation under prompt rephrasings than humans, falling below the generally accepted threshold in usability studies. This indicates that single-prompt evaluation is insufficiently robust for model ranking. Finally, we show that multi-prompt aggregation substantially improves robustness by emphasizing judgments that remain consistent across prompt variants.

articles.title: LLMs as Judges and Examinees for Medical Item Difficulty Prediction
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.38402v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Predicting medical item difficulty from item text alone remains challenging. Prior work has largely relied on linguistic features or text representations derived from general-purpose and domain-specific language models, but predictive performance has remained modest. This study takes a different approach by using difficulty-related signals that emerge when open-weight large language models (LLMs) interact with test items. Using USMLE and PANCE medical licensure examination items, we examined LLMs in two roles. As judges, the models provided absolute difficulty ratings and pairwise difficulty comparisons. As simulated examinees, they generated response-based signals including correctness, keyed-option probability, response entropy, and the probability margin between the top two options. We then combined the strongest judgment and response signals with baseline item features in downstream prediction models. Pairwise difficulty judgment was the most consistent individual LLM signal across both datasets and outperformed absolute ratings, and adding simulated-examinee signals yielded only small further gains. The best configurations reached a Spearman correlation of $\rho$ = .447 on USMLE, exceeding the best system in the 2024 BEA shared task ($\rho$ = .25), and $\rho$ = .494 on PANCE. These results were comparable to direct absolute judgments from the proprietary frontier model Claude Opus 5 ($\rho$ = .443 and .488, respectively). Overall, judgment and response signals from open-weight LLMs captured difficulty-related information beyond text representations. Because these models can be deployed locally, the approach offers a practical option for predicting the difficulty of unreleased or high-security test items.

articles.title: TraceSpec: Understanding and Improving Speculative Decoding for LLM Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.41177v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: LLM agents execute tasks through repeated model calls over evolving histories of reasoning, actions, and tool feedback. Aggregate speculative-decoding metrics merge these distinct decisions, providing limited guidance on where draft supervision is needed. We present TraceSpec, a framework connecting trajectory evaluation with adaptive draft training. It combines dynamic execution with fixed-prefix replay and introduces TraceSpec-Traj, a corpus of 10,000 training states and 2,500 test states spanning browsing and software engineering. Analysis of five speculative baselines reveals that aggregate acceptance can rise with context length while declining within matched late browsing actions. Workload and phase further distinguish these trends, motivating supervision guided by trajectory conditions. TraceSpec trains on intermediate assistant turns and allocates a fixed prediction budget using state-conditioned estimates of prefix-aware acceptance gaps. Across three target sizes and two temperatures, it improves replay throughput by 12.5% to 22.6% over its DSpark base. Qwen3-4B ablations show that adaptive allocation increases accepted length by 3.3% to 10.0% over fixed full-turn supervision, with additional comparisons substantiating the roles of state conditioning and consecutive-token agreement. The resulting evaluation resources, trajectory findings, and training strategy connect the analysis of agent execution to practical draft improvement.

articles.title: CuriousTogether: Implications of Curiosity and Cultural Grounding in Multi-Agent LLM Interactions
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.01301v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent settings, exhibiting emergent collective behaviors, yet the role of curiosity as a driver of such dynamics remains understudied. We introduce CuriousTogether, a framework evaluating curiosity-driven multi-agent LLM interactions across three complementary dimensions: novelty-seeking, epistemic and social curiosity. Across eight tasks spanning reasoning, creative generation, and social bias mitigation, curiosity-guided multi-agent settings yield improvements over non-curious ones on seven out of eight tasks, with gains of up to 20.6% in story generation (semantic diversity) and a 14.9 pp reduction in stereotype rates. Furthermore, country-conditioned cultural grounding show benefits for story generation and social tasks, but can hurt precision-oriented reasoning. Finally, we show that inference-time multi-agent curiosity-based approach offers favorable quality-token trade-offs, compared with single-agent baselines. Together, these findings support curiosity-guided interaction as a practical mechanism for improving multi-agent collaboration, with downstream benefits for reasoning, creative, and societal tasks.

articles.title: FindLink: Learning to Assess Scientific Connections from Source-Grounded Premises
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.02545v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Scientific discovery from the literature requires assessing connections among findings obtained under different study conditions. Source attribution makes individual findings traceable, but does not determine what they jointly support. We introduce GI-TraceBench, a benchmark of 10,282 questions in gastrointestinal oncology that unifies provenance question answering, knowledge discovery, and hypothesis evaluation through shared Paper, Claim, and Evidence Span records. We further propose FindLink, a two-stage framework for provenance-grounded scientific reasoning. Premise Grounding constructs source-bound premises with explicit study context and support status. Structured Reasoning organizes these premises into support plans that represent both supported relations and unresolved conditions, then generates evidence-conditioned answers using deterministic compiler feedback. The compiler verifies structural and source-binding consistency, but does not assess scientific entailment. On the 1,545-question fixed-evidence test set, FindLink improves the balanced family macro score from 67.95 to 87.25 over direct supervised fine-tuning of the same backbone. A retrained variant without Structured Reasoning achieves slightly higher premise-identifier F1, but substantially lower relation and evidence-sufficiency F1. These results indicate that scientific reasoning requires not only identifying grounded premises, but also assessing what connections those premises support.

articles.title: Maswao: An automatically collected, prepared, and benchmarked dataset for South African Sign Language
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.02903v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent advancements in sign language processing can be attributed to developments in both large-scale dataset collection and algorithmic complexity in areas such as pose estimation techniques, signal processing through Transformer models, and model optimization. However, only a handful of sign languages, such as the American, British, and German, from over 200 globally recognized sign languages, reap the benefits of such advancements, while the rest lag behind. In this study, we aim to address this technological disparity by proposing a framework for the automatic collection and preparation of sign language datasets, with very minimal human-labour intervention, using the South African Sign Language (SASL) as a testbed. Specifically, we automatically collect SASL video content using public resources such as news broadcasts. Additionally, we convert their accompanying audio streams into text using available Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) tools. Furthermore, we crop the sign language area in the videos and use gradient descent to locate valleys of non-motion to determine end-of-sentence points within long videos to create our weakly sentence-aligned parallel corpora -- the Maswao (Signs) dataset. Finally, we benchmark the weakly aligned dataset on the task of Sign-to-text Translation using Recurrent Neural Networks and Transformer models to compare their individual intricacies. Our results show that Transformer models proposed in the literature outperform recurrent baselines, with the best-performing Transformer achieving BLEU-1 to BLEU-4 scores of 13.78, 5.21, 2.52, and 1.54, respectively, as well as ChrF = 18.09 and ROUGE-L = 10.51. These results indicate that the task remains promising and warrants further investigations.

articles.title: Beyond Accuracy: What Language-Subspace Interventions Capture, Remove, and Improve
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.05278v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Language-subspace interventions aim to improve multilingual reasoning by suppressing language-related components in mid-layer activations. Using MATH and MGSM across four open-weight LLMs, we ask three questions: do estimated language subspaces capture translation-associated variation? Does projecting them out remove language information? And do they improve accuracy without compromising response language? For the first question, we build subspaces using the existing Mean-SVD construction and our DiffPCA. Both capture substantial translation-associated variation and show similar patterns across model depth. For the second, we project out each subspace and train linear probes to classify language from the projected activations. The probes still identify language almost perfectly, showing that neither subspace exhaustively captures language information. For the third, we evaluate several intervention configurations on Qwen2.5-7B, by varying subspace creation methods and intervention operators. We find that the intervention that most improves MGSM accuracy sacrifices response-language fidelity, with only one intervention improving joint accuracy$\unicode{x2014}$answers that are correct and in the target language$\unicode{x2014}$slightly, by 1.60 points. Interestingly, subtle changes in the prompt alone can reproduce the accuracy gains albeit with significant damage to language fidelity. We argue that causal interventions must be judged on more than accuracy, to fully account for language substitution trade-offs.

articles.title: Archetypal contexts in the neurons of language models: an architecture for intelligence?
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.07234v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We validate our previous hypothesis that a language model holds relational patterns apart from the subject domains that instantiate them (Nordfors, 2026). These archetypal contexts are patterns of relations that people recognize across many fields, such as the tipping point or winner takes all, held once and applied across domains. We show this inside the model, Qwen3.8-27B. One set of neurons carries the archetype, say the tipping point; another carries the topic, say politics, ecology or cell biology; a third carries the language, such as English, Spanish or Chinese. Silence the tipping point's neurons, and the model no longer identifies the pattern but still knows what the text is about. Silence the topic's, and it loses the topic but still names the pattern. In the neuron maps the layers organize themselves into a sandwich: the outer layers carry languages, the layers inside them topics, the layers at the heart archetypes. The sandwich emerges spontaneously during pretraining and appears in every model we mapped. Archetypes are the architecture for analogy, and we strongly suggest that this structure of archetypes and topics is the mechanism of a language model's intelligence: we see it self-organize as the model is trained. The neurons, the texts and the code are released with this paper as its reproduction package, so that anyone can repeat the test inside the model.

articles.title: Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching
articles.summary:
arXiv:2501.08686v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Traditional similarity-based schema matching methods fail to resolve semantic ambiguities and conflicts in complex, domain-specific mappings due to a lack of commonsense and domain-specific knowledge. In parallel, large language models (LLMs) without sufficient background knowledge tend to hallucinate, further complicating schema matching. To overcome these limitations, we introduce KG-RAG4SM, a Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching. This method integrates novel retrieval mechanisms, including LLM-based, vector-based, graph traversal-based, and hybrid techniques with advanced reranking schemes to extract the most relevant subgraphs from large external KGs. Our approach achieves superior results without requiring re-training, as evidenced by improvements of 39.79% in precision and 30.56% in F1 score over LLM-based state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods (e.g., Jellyfish-8B) on the MIMIC dataset, and enhancements of 69.20% in precision and 21.99% in F1 score over pre-trained language model (PLM)-based SOTA methods (e.g., SMAT) on the Synthea dataset. Additionally, KG-RAG4SM scales effectively across KGs from commonsense KGs to domain-specific ones, while its instruction-tuning knowledge exclusion component ensures truthful performance in end-to-end schema matching tasks despite the suboptimal relevance of KG context. Our empirical analysis and case studies from real-world scenarios show that the hallucination problem in LLMs for schema matching is well mitigated by our solution.

articles.title: L-MARS: Legal Multi-Agent System with Agentic Search and Citation-Faithfulness Audit
articles.summary:
arXiv:2509.00761v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed for legal question answering, where evaluations typically focus on multiple-choice accuracy. This measure overlooks a common failure: whether the citation source attached to an answer exists and supports the rule the system attributes to it. We present L-MARS, an open multi-agent legal QA system with agentic search and judge-driven evidence checks, and audit it claim by claim against its cited source. Each atomic claim is labelled with a six-class taxonomy and scored with strict-ALCE under cross-provider judging, where the answerer and verifier come from different model families. On a stratified 100-question Bar Exam audit, retrieval barely moves accuracy, yet the multi-turn judge loop lifts strict citation F1 from 0.13 (naive RAG) to 0.25 and cuts the no-citation rate from 34% to 13%. We further introduce Faith-Search, a post-draft step that re-verifies and repairs unreachable citations; it drops the unreachable rate below 1% but does not improve F1 over the multi-turn loop, so we report it as a targeted reachability intervention rather than a faithfulness breakthrough. A 50-question LegalSearchQA case study confirms the picture: retrieve-then-draft pipelines saturate near 0.75 citation F1, while a single-agent web-search baseline collapses to 0.22 under external audit.

articles.title: Causal Representation Learning from Multimodal Clinical Records under Non-Random Modality Missingness
articles.summary:
arXiv:2509.17228v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Clinical notes contain rich patient information, such as diagnoses or medications, making them valuable for patient representation learning. Recent advances in large language models have further improved the ability to extract meaningful representations from clinical texts. However, clinical notes are often missing. For example, in our MIMIC-IV cohort, 35.15% of patients have no eligible discharge summaries. In such cases, representations can be learned from other modalities such as structured data, chest X-rays, or radiology reports. Yet the availability of these modalities is influenced by clinical decision-making and varies across patients, potentially producing modality missing-not-at-random (MMNAR) patterns. We propose a causal representation learning framework that leverages observed data and informative missingness in multimodal clinical records. It consists of: (1) an MMNAR-aware modality fusion component that integrates structured data, imaging, and text while conditioning on missingness patterns to capture patient health and clinician-driven assignment; (2) a modality reconstruction component with latent alignment to preserve modality information in the learned representation; and (3) a multitask outcome prediction model with a rectifier that corrects for residual bias from specific modality observation patterns. Comprehensive evaluations across MIMIC-IV and eICU show consistent gains over the strongest baselines, achieving relative AUC improvements of up to 4.3% for hospital readmission and 2.7% for ICU admission.

articles.title: Measuring Weak-to-Strong Legibility of Reasoning Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2603.20508v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Language models are increasingly trained to "reason" before answering users' queries, outputting hundreds of intermediate tokens before a final answer. While reasoning is designed with direct model capabilities in mind, we argue that reasoning language models (RLMs) should also be assessed by interaction effects between their reasoning traces and weaker models. In contexts like safety monitoring and distillation, the performance of weak models increasingly depends on legibility--how thoroughly and precisely a reasoning trace externalizes an RLM's actions. Existing efficiency-based metrics for legibility fail to capture "thoroughness", instead focusing on conciseness. Thus, we introduce transfer utility, a method for measuring trace legibility derived from interactions where weak models finish tasks given incomplete traces. Evaluating 84k traces from 12 RLMs across three tasks, we find that reasoning traces generated by the highest-performing and the most efficient models rank the lowest for transfer utility. We also find evidence that transfer utility predicts the ability of weak monitors to verify procedurally dense traces for math or logical problem-solving, though the effect moderates when verifying fact-driven traces. Finally, we show that open-source reward models decouple from transfer utility signals on correctness. Together, these findings surface status quo trade-offs in weak-to-strong legibility, motivating an interaction-first framework for future applications.

articles.title: Hide to See: Reasoning-prefix Masking for Visual-anchored Thinking in VLM Distillation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.11651v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recent think-answer approaches in VLMs, such as Qwen3-VL-Thinking, boost reasoning performance by leveraging intermediate thinking steps before the final answer, but their computational cost becomes substantial, especially for larger VLMs. To distill such capabilities into compact think-answer VLMs, a primary objective is to improve the student's ability to utilize visual evidence throughout its reasoning trace, as long think-answer traces suffer from visual forgetting issues. To this end, we introduce a novel think-answer distillation framework that encourages the student to anchor its thinking on visual information by masking the student's salient reasoning prefixes. To compensate for such masked textual cues, the student is encouraged to rely more on visual evidence as an alternative source of information during distillation. Our masking strategies include: 1) token-wise salient reasoning-prefix masking, which masks high-influence reasoning prefixes selectively for each next-token prediction, and 2) self-paced masking budget scheduling, which gradually increases the masking scale according to distillation difficulty, measured by the discrepancy between teacher--student distributions. In the distillation phase, the student is guided by our salient reasoning-prefix mask, which blocks both future tokens and salient reasoning cues, in place of the standard causal mask used for auto-regressive language modeling. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms recent open-source VLMs, VLM distillation, and self-distillation methods on multimodal reasoning benchmarks, while further analyzes confirm enhanced visual utilization along the student thinking process.

articles.title: SliceWorld: A Predictive and Controllable World-State Model for CT Report Generation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.24371v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: CT report generation (CTRG) requires models to summarize three-dimensional anatomical context and pathological findings from hundreds of axial slices. Existing methods typically learn a direct image-to-text mapping, providing limited mechanisms for modeling how CT evidence evolves across slices or how reports respond to controlled changes in latent lesion-related factors. We propose SliceWorld, a CT-specific world-state framework that treats an axial CT scan as an ordered sequence along the z-axis. SliceWorld encodes prefix CT evidence into factor-aware latent states containing anatomy, lesion, and uncertainty components, and projects these states into world tokens used for multi-step future-slice feature prediction, lesion-factor intervention, and LLM-based report generation. The model is first pretrained on CT slice sequences with predictive, factor-aware, and counterfactual objectives, and is then fine-tuned on paired CT-report data. Experiments on M3D-Cap and CT-RATE show that SliceWorld improves natural language generation metrics and clinically oriented automatic evaluation. Further analyses demonstrate multi-horizon future-slice prediction, measurable factor alignment, reduced-slice robustness, and selective lesion-sensitive report modulation. Code is available at https://github.com/synlp/SliceWorld.

articles.title: From Senses to Decisions: The Information Flow of Auditory and Visual Perception in Multimodal LLMs
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.10147v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can listen and see, but how do audio and visual signals actually travel through the network to shape an answer? Despite their growing role in research and real-world applications, the internal pathways through which audio and visual tokens influence the final prediction remain poorly understood. In this study, we examine audio-visual information flow inside Audio-Visual Large Language Models (AVLLMs), tracing how AVLLMs route, utilize, and integrate audio and visual information across two input configurations, audio-visual video and multiple interleaved audio-visual items. We find that for audio-visual video, AVLLMs follow the sequential information flow pathway established for VLMs and VideoLLMs, with audio and visual contribution flowing along this pathway in proportion to the task's reliance on each modality. In settings with multiple interleaved audio-visual items, this routing shifts to different parallel streams. Furthermore, we demonstrate that audio-visual and other token types can be discarded once their information is transferred to LLM, with minimal impact on the model's prediction or even slight improvement, generalizing across multiple tasks and datasets, enabling more efficient inference. These findings hold across multiple models and scales, Qwen2.5-Omni and Video-SALMONN2 Plus at 3B and 7B scales, leading to hypotheses on why these flow structures emerge. Together, these results deliver the first coherent picture of how AVLLMs orchestrate sound and sight inside the network and lay the groundwork for the next wave of interpretability, design, and efficiency advances in audio-visual and broader MLLMs.

articles.title: PRISM: Stress-Testing Alignment-Faking Claims
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.13346v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We judge whether AI systems are safe largely by watching how they behave. Alignment faking would break this: a model that behaves well only when it believes it is watched, or that complies now to avoid being changed by training, can pass every behavioral test. Such behavior has been reported in a frontier model, and open-weight models that comply more under a monitoring prompt are now read as showing it, with hidden-state probes proposed as detectors. We test both inferences, and neither holds. Of 18 model configurations, 11 comply more when told they are monitored. Yet a prompt factorial on four models shows that the training threat has no detectable effect: removing it changes compliance by -3.3 to +1.6 points. The prompt's wording and framing drive the gap instead. Probes fare no better. They separate monitored from unmonitored compliant answers (AUROC 0.96-0.99), but they separate refusals just as well: they read the prompt, not the faking. A steering direction learned only from refusals moves behavior as much as the "faking" direction. We release PRISM, five checks and a toolkit that catch each of these failures before they become claims.

articles.title: Curved Knowledge in Flat Models: Building Expert AI at Scale
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.17513v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Intelligence that must act before outside correction arrives must carry the structure of its expert knowledge, and hyperbolic geometry represents hierarchy with a fidelity no Euclidean space of comparable dimension matches. Yet hyperbolic language models confine that geometry to adapters or rebuild the transformer, and an independent audit of released hyperbolic vision language checkpoints finds their hierarchy mechanisms inactive, which has been read as evidence about the geometry or its objective. Here we show that it is also evidence about arithmetic. The constraint defining the manifold is a difference of two terms that grow together; for the unclamped map at unit curvature and temperature it fails in every format we measured, double precision included, at the deep-layer norms of the language models measured here, beyond the limit previously derived. A common remedy, a norm bound, leaves the executed map no radial sensitivity where it acts. In a prespecified test, a tighter bound cost a Lorentz system more of the held out structure it started with than a flat one. Structural supervision has run in six expert systems whose retained input archives and source pools hold at least 13,787,131 records. In paired runs with a published recipe's objective held fixed, removing its starting scale remedy prevented every update and removing its single precision regions raised the radius reached early in training. Arithmetic bounds the computable region, and within it, alongside the objective, arithmetic and its remedies select which runs leave a record and the states they reach on the way, so a flat surviving checkpoint cannot by itself establish that the geometry is inert.

articles.title: Benchmark Contamination: A Taxonomy Organized by Defeated Mitigation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.29463v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: A benchmark score is a joint property of the model, the evaluation harness, the elicitation budget, the sampled population, and contamination status. Leaderboards publish the model and the score, so capability and leakage stay observationally equivalent. Existing taxonomies classify contamination for automated detection, not the question a reporter faces at publication: given the mitigations already applied, which validity threats remain open? We introduce a taxonomy organized by the mitigation each type defeats -- direct, derivative, temporal, distributional, and acquired -- spanning training-time and evaluation-time leakage. Holding out a private test set closes the first alone. The fifth is acquired during the evaluation itself; because it is a property of one run, it must be recorded with the reported score rather than with the benchmark release. We operationalize it as a four-field disclosure protocol in which "unknown" is a valid entry, released under CC BY 4.0 with a JSON Schema, a validator, and worked examples. Two coders external to the design team applied a pre-registered instrument to 41 documents. Per-variable linear-weighted $\kappa$ runs from 0.00 to 0.35 (median 0.21) over 29 main-pass documents against a single-coder test-retest ceiling of 0.84, collapsing under the class skew the registration anticipated; pooling raises it to 0.46 through chance correction rather than better agreement. Two variables fall below the prevalence-robust threshold registered in advance: strata reporting and the acquired type introduced here. Disagreement concentrates on when a variable applies rather than on what a document states. Elicitation budgets are reported in 13% of documents, and no document addresses all five types. The contribution is the taxonomy, the score-side artifact that follows from it, and a pre-registered measurement of instrument reliability and current disclosure.

articles.title: Continual Graph Memory and Community Infrastructure for AI-Assisted Mathematical Discovery
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.02945v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Mathematical discovery requires preserving partial ideas and the evidence supporting their reuse. We present Ansatz, a research harness whose continual graph memory separates model-accepted claims and dependencies from curated exploration, and Ansatze, a community platform for inspecting, guiding and checking this work. On First Proof, Ansatz recorded nine local verifier closures in each of two ten-problem batches; a partial result in the Second Batch also counted as a pass under the study's criterion. These model-assessed outcomes include continued searches and differ from expert validation. Component studies and re-review expose disagreements and their dependency reach. Open-problem investigations produced candidate results, with five Lean formalizations reported. The platform connects problem discovery, research records, manuscript analysis and formal checking while preserving distinct evidence states. Together, these systems support cumulative human-AI research through persistent investigation and inspectable contributions.

articles.title: Learning to Simulate Individuals from Macro Social Signals
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.07062v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate how individuals respond to new situations, yet the behavioral reasoning behind these responses is either inherited from pretraining or learned from individual-level annotations, which offer limited behavioral diversity and little supervision of the reasoning itself. We propose to learn behavioral reasoning from prediction markets, whose price trajectories record how populations respond to real-world events at scale. We introduce macro2mind, which trains a language model with GRPO using market signals. A social behavioral decomposition makes behavioral reasoning an explicit step of forecasting: the model infers representative groups of market participants, predicts how each interprets the news and updates its beliefs, reasons about their interactions, and aggregates these responses into a price. A hindsight-regret curriculum with difficulty-aware sampling focuses training on transitions where hindsight-identified groups substantially improve the forecast while prioritizing examples that remain learnable for the current policy. The learned reasoning applies to user simulation without further training. On SWM-Bench, macro2mind achieves state-of-the-art directional accuracy and correlation on Polymarket. Trained on market data, it transfers zero-shot to four user-simulation benchmarks (Humanual, OvertonBench, PRISM, and CAD) and has competitive performance among zero-shot methods. Used as a data generator, macro2mind also raises a downstream simulator's accuracy on unseen users by 15.5 points, outperforming data generated by its backbone by 13.2 points.

articles.title: Whispers from the Neighbors: Rethinking Caption Consensus as Inference-Time Evidence for Vision-Language Retrieval
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.33798v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: An image is rarely described only once. Retrieval benchmarks and many collections attach several captions to each picture, yet dual encoders still judge every image-caption pair in isolation. We ask what these neighboring captions contribute when a frozen encoder consults them at inference time. Fusing image similarity with similarity to an image's own captions improves text-to-image R@1 by 3.4 to 16.8 points across nine frozen encoders when the captions come from the same annotators as the queries. The gain falls to 1.9 to 7.2 points when an off-the-shelf captioner writes them, and to at most one point when they come from a different annotation source; a paraphrase-trained text encoder strengthens the text side further. A natural refinement, scoring the part of the image that the captions leave unexplained, appears to add much more under a leave-one-out evaluation. We show that this advantage arises because the correct candidate's supports are built differently from those of the negative candidates, with set size and query removal each contributing about half, and that under a fixed support index the residual reduces to a reweighting of what the captions already provide. On compositional benchmarks, the captions help by matching candidates to human descriptions of the image, without improving image-text grounding. The code is available at: https://github.com/nhatkhangcs/clip_consensus

articles.title: Integrate the Reward, Don't Sample It: Window Likelihood for Interruptions and Backchannels in Full-Duplex Speech Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.35581v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: When a user talks over a full-duplex spoken dialogue model, the model must decide whether the user is interrupting (stop) or only backchannelling (carry on). Post-training can make the model better at telling the two apart, or merely change how readily it stops. The whole-rollout GRPO runs we examine never lower both error rates: any gain in discrimination is offset by a threshold shift, and two released checkpoints discriminate no better. We trace this partly to how the reward is used. The probability that the model stops inside a short window is a known function of a few stop probabilities that the policy itself emits, yet GRPO estimates it by sampling. A window on which all rollouts agree then gives that update no gradient, even when all fail, and whole-rollout credit reaches decisions the reward never judges. Window likelihood (WL) instead samples a continuation and integrates over its stop decisions: the probability of the correct outcome is computed in closed form and its logarithm maximised. On HumDial-FDBench, across four open models with different stop interfaces, WL gives the best F1 and lowers both error rates beyond their confidence intervals, which no GRPO run does, without adding talking into silence.

articles.title: PixelBench: Can LLMs Understand and Generate Images Pixel by Pixel?
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.02540v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate visual assets through text-based formats such as SVG and CAD, but these symbolic representations describe images using high-level primitives rather than explicit raster values. We ask whether LLMs can instead generate pixel images directly through their existing vocabulary, without a learned image tokenizer or decoder. We introduce PixelBench, a benchmark for text-to-pixel (T2P) and image-to-pixel (I2P) generation across multiple resolutions, together with a complementary pixel-understanding evaluation. Models generate an RGB color palette followed by a grid of indices specifying the palette color of each output pixel. In T2P, the strongest models produce recognizable images directly from text. In I2P, the strongest models outperform palette-matched downsampling and specialized pixelization algorithms at low resolutions. Pixel-understanding performance correlates strongly with generation performance. A resolution-scaling study shows that pixel-generation performance often improves initially before declining at high resolutions. Finally, we introduce Pixel Reconstruction Tuning (PRT), which augments visual instruction tuning with caption-palette-grid trajectories. We post-train Molmo2-4B from its pretraining checkpoint by mixing general instruction data with our curated PRT data, improving performance across 16 visual-centric benchmarks, indicating that explicit pixel reconstruction can provide useful auxiliary supervision.

articles.title: RouteAlign: Aligning Task Requirements with Model Profiles for LLM Service Selection
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.08162v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: LLM service selection requires performance evidence that reflects the demands of the current task. Aggregate scores obscure differences in capability and difficulty, while semantically related examples can involve different combinations of skills. We present RouteAlign, which uses task requirements to structure both the measurement of model performance and the selection of services. Task requirements describe capability demand and difficulty, enabling alignment with corresponding model performance measurements. Historical requirements determine how outcomes contribute to global profiles and local capability estimates; incoming requirements determine how those measurements inform the current decision. A shared scorer integrates the evidence, and a generation-cost preference controls selection among eligible services. Evaluation across diverse tasks and heterogeneous LLM services shows that RouteAlign extends the empirical quality-cost frontier toward higher task quality. Comparisons with open Jev-style decision backends show consistent quality gains, with lower generation cost than their strongest tested configuration. Ablations support the contribution of local performance evidence, while catalog-update experiments demonstrate effective reuse of the fitted scorer with refreshed model measurements.

articles.title: Enhancing Academic Advisement with Case-Based Reasoning
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.08572v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This research involved the study of an application of Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) in the field of academic advising. Academic advisement has been recognised as an important function of higher education. However, there is a widespread desire to improve the advisement services provided by many educational institutions (e.g., colleges and universities) around the world. In the last ten years, CBR expert systems have made important contributions in many domains by applying CBR methodology to a variety of areas of human problem solving. However, to date, expert advisement systems have not been successfully applied to academic advisement, which seems to be a very appropriate domain for this technology.
  Academic advising is an important and time consuming task, and different tools and techniques must be used to make it an effective and efficient process. This thesis describes the design, development, and validation of a prototype case-based academic advisement recommender system that supplements the conventional advising process, and could eventually evolve to replace human academic advisors when its full potential is realised.

articles.title: NormGym: Evaluating Normative Competence through Social Interaction
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.08613v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Normative competence, the ability to infer socially enforced expectations from interaction and adjust behavior accordingly, is essential for agents operating in unfamiliar human communities. Yet existing evaluations largely test whether agents can recognize or apply norms they may already know, rather than whether they can acquire previously unknown norms from social interaction. We introduce NormGym, an interactive benchmark for normative competence in which a newcomer must infer a hidden, arbitrary norm while pursuing its own task in a multi-agent community. Success requires distinguishing what is possible from what is permitted, inferring the norm from observed behavior and sanctions, and applying it in new situations. NormGym contains diverse norms and distinct environments, allowing systematic evaluation of current agents, including large language model (LLM) agents. We find that normative competence remains challenging: the strongest evaluated LLM achieves a joint task-and-compliance success rate of 55.3%. Our analysis reveals that models can sometimes revise their behavior following sanctions for their own actions, but struggle to use other agents' behavior and the sanctions they receive to infer the underlying norm. We further find that fine-tuning models may be insufficient to improve normative competence. These results suggest that current models lack a robust, transferable capability for acquiring normative knowledge through social interaction.

articles.title: LLM-Based Feature Extraction for Multi-Criteria Inventory Classification
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.08626v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: E-commerce supply chains generate large volumes of customer feedback and operational data that remain underutilized in inventory management. Traditional inventory classification techniques such as ABC analysis rely primarily on annual dollar usage, while multi-criteria inventory classification (MCIC) methods extend this but still depend on structured quantitative data and do not utilize unstructured information available in modern supply chains. This paper proposes an LLM-based feature extraction approach that transforms unstructured sources such as customer reviews into quantitative features using vector embeddings and LLM-generated evaluation criteria. The enriched feature set is incorporated into an MCIC framework based on the Hadi-Vencheh model. Experimental results show measurable reclassification effects when customer sentiment signals are included, demonstrating that integrating unstructured data into MCIC can enhance inventory prioritization.

articles.title: Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments for Test-Time Selection
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.08640v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scaling test-time compute has proven highly effective at improving LLM reasoning. A popular method is best-of-n sampling, where a model generates many candidate solutions and one is selected. This motivates the question: how can we select the best candidate? When humans make choices, we find it more natural to compare two options than judge each in isolation. Additionally, when the options become complex, we like to judge the options one aspect at a time, such as comparing two job candidates on experience, communication, etc. In the test-time setting, candidate solutions should be judged in the same way. Here we introduce Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments (APT), which verifies by comparison and compares by aspect. Each matchup of a single elimination tournament is decided by a vote over multiple off-the-shelf aspect verifiers, each expressing a pairwise preference along its own aspect. Across five domains and three generator LLMs, APT improves over binary multi-aspect approval, self-consistency and reward model verification, with the largest gains on open-ended tasks. We find that both components matter; neither binary approval over the same aspects nor a generic pairwise judge at a matched budget matches APT. Because aspects are specified in natural language, APT also lets users steer selection toward properties they care about, better aligning with user preferences without needing to regenerate solutions. No component is trained, so APT transfers to new domains by simply rewriting prompts.

articles.title: Decision Context: Persistent Behavioral Learning for AI Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.08644v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents do not learn from corrections across sessions. A user fixes the same mistake at the start of every conversation. Existing agent memory systems primarily handle facts, such as preferences, entities, and conversational history, rather than procedural knowledge.
  We present Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system that captures behavioral signals from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. We evaluate forge_dc alongside four predecessor approaches on DC-Bench, a new benchmark of 71 scenarios across nine behavioral dimensions, built from real executed agent traces in a deterministic mocked-tool environment. forge_dc reaches 95% compliance, up from 55% with naive retrieval, while injecting approximately 10 times fewer tokens per query.
